name: Poland
governanceModel: EU member implementing the AI Act via a national Act on AI Systems and a new supervisor (KRiBSI), alongside a sovereign-model and data-centre push
debateTopics: Distributed EU AI Act enforcement and the new KRiBSI commission

overview:
Poland has positioned itself as Central and Eastern Europe's most ambitious AI hub, combining a growing hyperscale data-centre market, EuroHPC-funded 'AI factories', a state-backed sovereign language model (PLLuM) and an increasingly active regulatory agenda. Policy is coordinated by the Ministry of Digital Affairs under Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski, with Deputy Minister Dariusz Standerski leading much of the day-to-day AI work.

On 31 March 2026 the Council of Ministers adopted a draft Act on Artificial Intelligence Systems to transpose the EU AI Act into Polish law and establish the Commission for the Development and Security of Artificial Intelligence (KRiBSI) as the national supervisory authority -- an independent body administratively serviced by the Ministry of Digital Affairs. The EU AI Act's general-purpose AI obligations took effect on 2 August 2026, with the AI Office in Brussels supervising the largest general-purpose models directly. Industrially, Poland has attracted large hyperscaler commitments (Microsoft, Google and AWS all operate or are expanding cloud capacity around Warsaw), secured two EuroHPC AI factories (PIAST in Poznan and Gaia in Krakow), and taken a symbolic equity stake in voice-AI company ElevenLabs -- founded by two Varsovians -- while launching an 'AI Lab Poland' to grow domestic startups.

currentDirection.summary: Poland is moving from strategy to enforcement architecture: it has adopted a national Act on AI Systems creating the KRiBSI supervisor and aligned with the EU AI Act's 2 August 2026 general-purpose AI milestone, while simultaneously loosening barriers to investment through sandboxes and heavy data-centre expansion. The net direction is a more formal regulatory regime layered onto an aggressive growth push.

recentDevelopments.text: President Karol Nawrocki signed Poland's Act on Artificial Intelligence Systems into law on 24 July 2026, following parliamentary passage; published in the Journal of Laws on 27 July, it enters into force (as a rule) on 11 August 2026, formally establishing the Commission for the Development and Security of Artificial Intelligence (KRiBSI) as the sole national market-surveillance authority and single EU contact point under the AI Act — though KRiBSI still has to be formally constituted before it begins operating.
Poland entered the race to host one of the EU-backed AI 'gigafactories', reflecting its ambition to anchor large-scale AI compute in Central Europe on top of its existing EuroHPC AI factories.

Vinci, the venture arm of Poland's state development bank BGK, invested about USD 11m in voice-AI company ElevenLabs (founded by Varsovians Mati Staniszewski and Piotr Dabkowski) and launched 'AI Lab Poland' to support early-stage Polish AI startups.

The EU AI Act's general-purpose AI obligations took effect on 2 August 2026; in Poland the new Act on AI Systems is intended to designate national competent authorities and stand up the KRiBSI commission, which reporting suggests could begin operating later in 2026.

The Council of Ministers adopted the draft Act on Artificial Intelligence Systems, transposing the EU AI Act into Polish law and establishing the Commission for the Development and Security of Artificial Intelligence (KRiBSI) as national supervisory authority, with powers of inspection and penalties and plans for an EU AI regulatory sandbox.

The Ministry of Digital Affairs issued guidelines for public administration on the use of AI, covering common use cases and deployment recommendations, as part of a wider Digitalisation Strategy running to 2035.

Poland anchored two of the EU's EuroHPC 'AI factories' -- PIAST in Poznan and the roughly EUR 70m Gaia AI factory in Krakow (reported to house over 1,000 GPUs) -- strengthening national AI research compute.

policyAndRegulation.title: Act on Artificial Intelligence Systems
policyAndRegulation.summary: Legislation transposing the EU AI Act into Polish law, adopted by the Council of Ministers on 31 March 2026, passed by Parliament and signed by President Karol Nawrocki on 24 July 2026. Published in the Journal of Laws on 27 July, it enters into force (as a rule) on 11 August 2026. It imposes risk-assessment, transparency and safeguard obligations on AI providers and deployers, and establishes the Commission for the Development and Security of Artificial Intelligence (KRiBSI) as the national supervisory authority -- an independent body administratively serviced by the Ministry of Digital Affairs, with powers to inspect and impose penalties -- and envisages an EU AI regulatory sandbox. KRiBSI must still be formally constituted before it begins operating.

policyAndRegulation.title: EU AI Act (general-purpose AI obligations)
policyAndRegulation.summary: As an EU member state, Poland is bound by the EU AI Act, whose general-purpose AI provisions and transparency duties took effect on 2 August 2026, with the AI Office in Brussels supervising the largest general-purpose models. National enforcement of many obligations depends on the domestic Act on AI Systems and KRiBSI once operational.

policyAndRegulation.title: AI Policy for Poland / Digitalisation Strategy to 2035
policyAndRegulation.summary: Poland's AI ambitions build on its earlier 'AI Policy for Poland' and a Digitalisation Strategy to 2035, which frames investment in compute (EuroHPC AI factories in Poznan and Krakow), public-sector AI adoption and skills. In March 2026 the Ministry of Digital Affairs issued practical AI-use guidelines for public administration.

researchEcosystem.summary: Polish AI research draws on strong mathematics and computer-science traditions across universities in Warsaw, Krakow, Poznan and Wroclaw, backed by state research institutes such as NASK and IDEAS NCBR, and increasingly by EuroHPC compute (the PIAST and Gaia AI factories). The flagship applied initiative is PLLuM, an open Polish large language model developed by a public consortium and hosted by the Ministry of Digital Affairs (CYFRAGOVPL), tailored to Polish and public-administration terminology.

notableGaps.note: Poland has no domestic frontier-scale commercial AI developer. PLLuM is a mid-sized (8-70B) open sovereign model rather than a frontier system, and ElevenLabs -- though Polish-founded -- is domiciled in London, so the 'emerging' label reflects public models and compute rather than a home-grown frontier champion.

As of early August 2026 the KRiBSI commission is not yet operational: the Act on AI Systems was signed by the President on 24 July 2026 and enters into force on 11 August 2026, but KRiBSI still has to be formally constituted and staffed before it can act, leaving national AI-Act enforcement mechanics not fully in place at the Act's main milestone.

Poland's rapid data-centre expansion is increasingly bounded by grid-connection and power-availability limits, a constraint repeatedly flagged in market analysis and central to whether its compute ambitions (including an EU gigafactory bid) can be realised.

debates.topic: Distributed EU AI Act enforcement and the new KRiBSI commission
debates.summary: Poland's choice to create a dedicated KRiBSI supervisor -- while housing it administratively within the Ministry of Digital Affairs -- has drawn debate over its independence and capacity.
debates.expanded: The Act on AI Systems designates KRiBSI as an independent authority with inspection and sanction powers, but critics note it is administratively serviced by the Ministry of Digital Affairs, raising questions about genuine independence and resourcing. Supporters argue a single, dedicated commission is clearer than the sectoral, multi-regulator models chosen by some other member states, and that pairing it with an early EU regulatory sandbox will help Polish firms adapt. The debate is partly about whether Poland can stand the body up quickly enough to matter for the AI Act's 2026 milestones.

debates.topic: Sovereign PLLuM model and public-sector AI adoption
debates.summary: PLLuM is promoted as a sovereign, Polish-language model for public services, but its practical competitiveness against global models is debated.
debates.expanded: PLLuM, developed by a public consortium and tailored to Polish and administrative language, is framed as a tool for trustworthy public-sector AI and linguistic sovereignty. Sceptics question whether an 8-70B open model can match commercial frontier systems for general capability, and whether public bodies will adopt it at scale versus off-the-shelf foreign models. The March 2026 public-administration AI guidelines are read as an attempt to channel adoption toward controlled, compliant use, with PLLuM as one option.

debates.topic: Data-centre boom versus grid and energy constraints
debates.summary: Hyperscaler investment has made Warsaw a leading CEE data-centre market, but grid connection and power supply are emerging as binding constraints.
debates.expanded: Microsoft, Google and AWS have all committed significant capacity around Warsaw, and Poland is bidding to host an EU AI gigafactory and building EuroHPC AI factories in Poznan and Krakow. Analysts increasingly argue that Poland's AI-compute ceiling will be set less by capital than by electricity availability and grid-connection timelines, echoing similar debates in Ireland. How Poland resolves the energy question is widely seen as decisive for its 'AI fortress' ambitions.
